This is a post to the follwoing discussion:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Nam3N7Y4b78/m/KdW-Oyo3AQAJ

This issue is an interesting one, raised a long time ago, but rarely discussed in the application of SEM. This is another related paper:

Yuan, K.-H., Ling, L., & Zhang, Z. (2024). Scale-invariance, equivariance and dependency of structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2024.2353168

The p-values reported by many SEM programs are, by default, the Wald p-values, which are not invariant to the parameterization of the model. The likelihood ratio test (LRT, a.k.a., chi-square difference test) p-value may be what we usually "really" want: If we fix a parameter to zero, is the model fit significantly different from the original model? This test yields the same p-value whether we fix a factor loading to one or fix the factor variances to one.

One obvious drawback of the LRT p-values is the computational cost. For Wald p-values, we don't have to fit another model. For LRT p-values, we need to fit one more model for each parameter.

To try making LRT p-values more accessible and address the issue with the Wald p-value, Mark Lai and I developed a package, semlrtp. This is a demonstration of how to use it:

https://sfcheung.github.io/semlrtp/articles/semlrtp.html

What it does is basically this:

For each free parameter with the LRT p-value requested:
- Fit a model with this parameter fixed to zero.
- Do the LRT.
- Report the p-value.

This is demonstration using a 3-factor CFA model:

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-19
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
library(semlrtp)

# Use fewer cases to demonstrate the functions
dat <- data_sem16[1:100, ]

mod <-
"
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
f3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 +x12
"

Two models are fitted, one with the first loadings fixed to one, the other with the factor variances fixed to one:

# Fix the first loadings to 1
fit_v1 <- sem(mod,
              dat)
# Fix the factor variances to 1
fit_v2 <- sem(mod,
              dat,
              std.lv = TRUE)

As expected, these two models have identical goodness of fit:

The function lrtp() can be used to compute the LRT p-values. By default, it only computes LRT p-values for regression coefficients ("~") and covariances ("~~", error variances and variances are excluded), to save computational cost. Therefore, I used op = c("=~", "~~" ) to compute LRT p-values for factor loadings too:

# Compute the LRT p-values
fit_v1_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v1,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))
fit_v2_lrtp <- lrtp(fit_v2,
                 op = c("=~", "~~"))

Not demonstrated above, the LRT p-values are also invariant to the choices of the items with their loadings fixed to one.

Being automatic comes at a cost. In trying the packages, we found cases in which the computation failed, because the model with a parameter fixed to zero failed to converge or had Heywood cases. We are working on this.

In any case, the function just does what we can do manually. Therefore, for these "difficult parameters," if we want to have the LRT p-values, we can fit the model manually and tweak some settings, such as the bounds.

There are cases in which the LRT p-value cannot be computed because the model with a parameter fixed to zero does not make sense and cannot be fitted. Nevertheless, for these parameters, perhaps the null hypothesis itself may not be meaningful anyway.

We are still exploring ways to improve this package. Comments and suggestions are welcome.

-- Shu Fai
